spec.title: Accepted by the API (202/s) per cell
spec.description: What k6 got a 202 for, split by cell (key mode and rate). The API only waits for Kafka, so this should follow the offered rate in both key modes. Surprising: it falls in one key mode only, because then the skew has reached the API and not only the consumers. k6 series are not marked stale after a run, so the last value can stay for minutes.

spec.title: Consumed by the whole group (events/s)
spec.description: Messages of completed chunks, all consumers added up. This is the throughput that counts. In tenant mode I look for a ceiling below the accepted rate while the hot partition is full; in event mode it should follow the accepted rate. Surprising: a ceiling in event mode, then something else (CPU, Postgres) is the limit.

spec.title: Lag per partition (messages)
spec.description: Log end offset minus committed offset, every partition (the same value on every consumer, so max by partition). Tenant mode above the ceiling: one line climbs, the others stay near 0. Event mode: all lines stay together and low. The sink polls this every second.

spec.title: Event freshness p99 (s)
spec.description: Time from the API receiving an event to the sink storing it. The growing backlog on the hot partition shows up here. The metric is not per partition, so it mixes hot and idle partitions: the p99 is dominated by the slow one. Surprising: a high p99 while all lags are 0.

spec.title: Share of the load on the busiest partition (%)
spec.description: Busiest partition's share of the new events (rate of the log end offset, topic k9-events). Tenant mode: about the hot tenant's 80 % plus whatever other tenants hash to the same partition. Event mode: about 100/6 = 17 %. Surprising: tenant mode far below 80 % (the load generator is not skewed) or event mode far above 17 %.

spec.title: Events written per partition (events/s)
spec.description: Rate of the log end offset of every partition of k9-events (what the producer puts in). Payloads have a fixed size, so bytes per partition are about this rate times the record size; the true bytes per partition are in captures/*.partition-bytes.txt. Look for: one line at about 80 % of the total (tenant) or six lines on top of each other (event). The kafka exporter scrape interval limits how fast the lines react.

spec.title: Events consumed per partition (events/s)
spec.description: Rate of the group's committed offset per partition. The hot partition is the one that flattens at its ceiling (chunk of 100 rows per 60 ms of work plus the insert time) while its written rate is above it. Surprising: a flat top at different heights for different runs, then the ceiling is not only the artificial delay.

spec.title: Lag per partition from the kafka exporter
spec.description: Same idea as the lag panel of row 1 but from the kafka exporter (separate measurement, slower scrape). If the two disagree a lot, one of the two pollers is stale.

spec.title: Consumed per consumer (events/s)
spec.description: Each consumer-sink process (port 8001 to 8003) owns 2 partitions. In tenant mode one consumer should be busy at its ceiling and the other two should take only what their partitions get. Which one is hot changes from run to run because the hash decides.

spec.title: Hot tenant share of the accepted requests (%)
spec.description: k9_hot_sent over all accepted requests: checks that the load generator really sends the planned share (80 %). The counters are added by K9 and exist in Prometheus only after a k6 run.

spec.title: Consumer-sink process CPU (cores)
spec.description: CPU used by each consumer-sink process, in cores. The artificial delay is sleeping, so a busy hot consumer is not CPU bound. Keep under about 0.7 of a core: above that the CPU, not the delay, would be the ceiling. Sinks 1 and 3 share one CPU.

spec.title: Sink CPUs busy (%, pinned CPUs)
spec.description: Host CPU use of the CPUs the consumer-sinks are pinned to (variable cpu_sinks). Keep under 70 %. Surprising: near 100 % in event mode at the top rate, then the throughput there is limited by CPU and that run says nothing about the key.

spec.title: Postgres commits per second
spec.description: Transactions committed in the eventpulse database. One chunk is one INSERT, so this is about consumed events divided by the chunk size. Surprising: a plateau in event mode when the sinks are not at their delay limit, then Postgres is the bottleneck.

spec.title: Sink DB write time p99 (s)
spec.description: Time of the INSERT of one chunk. The per-partition ceiling is chunk size divided by (delay + this), so this explains why the ceiling is a bit under 100 / 0.06 = 1667 events/s.

spec.title: Broker and API CPUs busy (%, pinned CPUs)
spec.description: Host CPU use of the CPUs of the brokers (cpu_brokers) and of the ingest-api (cpu_server). Not the limit in this experiment: the API only has to produce. Surprising: either near 100 %, then the producer side is limiting.

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations (must be 0)
spec.description: k6 could not start an iteration at the planned rate. A run with a value above 0 is discarded. k6 series are not marked stale after a run.

spec.title: k6 failed requests and 503s
spec.description: Rate of 503 answers from the API. Must be 0: with Kafka up and the API far below its knee (about 7,500 req/s) nothing should be refused.

spec.title: k6 CPUs busy (%, pinned CPUs)
spec.description: Host CPU use of the CPUs k6 is pinned to (cpu_k6). Keep under 70 %, otherwise the generator is the limit.

spec.title: API event loop lag (s)
spec.description: Event loop lag of the ingest-api. Above a few ms the API itself is struggling, which is not what this experiment is about.

spec.title: Partitions owned by the group (must be 6)
spec.description: Partitions owned, added up over the consumers. It must stay 6 for the whole run. A dip means a rebalance happened, and the lag of that run is then contaminated.

spec.title: Group rebalances in the window
spec.description: Increase of the rebalance counter per consumer. Each consumer joins once at the start of a run (a new process); after that it must not move. A step during the load means a consumer lost its partitions and the run is suspect.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: does the hot key cap throughput?
2. The mechanism: one partition full, the others idle
3. Resource view: where the work lands
4. Validity checks: can I trust this run?
